hints: Think about what must meet and overlap to make a stationary pattern - a single travelling wave just carries energy away, so what second wave is needed?
For a stable pattern with fixed nodes, what must be identical about the two overlapping waves, and in which directions must they travel?
walkthrough:
**What a stationary wave really is**
You are used to a travelling wave carrying energy along. A stationary wave looks still, with fixed nodes and antinodes. That can only happen if energy is not flowing away in one direction.

**Building it from two travelling waves**
Imagine a wave going right and an identical wave going left. Where they meet they add by superposition. Using $$v = f\lambda$$ both must have the same $f$, $\lambda$ and $v$ in the same medium, and ideally the same amplitude, so that at some points they always cancel to give nodes and at others they always reinforce to give antinodes.
Final answer: Two progressive waves of the same frequency (same wavelength and speed) and same amplitude travelling in opposite directions superpose.

hints: You are given speed $v$ in air and wavelength $\lambda$ for the sound - which universal wave relation links $v$, $f$ and $\lambda$?
Check units are already SI ($\text{m s}^{-1}$ and $\text{m}$) so you can rearrange directly for $f$ and calculate in $\text{Hz}$.
walkthrough:
**Choose the governing law**
For any progressive wave the speed is set by how many wavelengths pass per second: $$v = f\lambda$$ Here $v = 330\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and $\lambda = 0.18\text{ m}$.

**Rearrange and calculate**
$$f = \frac{v}{\lambda} = \frac{330}{0.18}$$ $$f \approx 1830\text{ Hz} \approx 1.8\times 10^{3}\text{ Hz}$$ Keep 2 or 3 significant figures.

hints: The time-base tells you how much time each horizontal cm represents. First find the time for one full cycle from your answer to (b)(i) using $T = 1/f$.
On Fig. 4.1 measure the horizontal length of one complete sine wave in cm (peak to next peak), then divide the period by that length.
walkthrough:
**Get the time for one oscillation**
From (b)(i) $f \approx 1.83\times 10^{3}\text{ Hz}$. $$T = \frac{1}{f} \approx \frac{1}{1830} \approx 5.5\times 10^{-4}\text{ s}$$ This is the real time of one sine wave you see.

**Convert screen distance to time**
Measure peak-to-peak horizontal distance on Fig. 4.1. It is about $8.0\text{ cm}$ for one full $\lambda$. Time-base setting is time per cm: $$\text{time-base} = \frac{T}{\text{length of one cycle}} \approx \frac{5.5\times 10^{-4}}{8.0} \approx 6.8\times 10^{-5}\text{ s cm}^{-1}$$ The method earns credit even if your cm reading differs slightly.

Final answer: Period $T = 1/1830 \approx 5.5 \times 10^{-4}\text{ s}$. One cycle $\approx 8.0\text{ cm}$ on screen, so time-base $\approx 5.5\times 10^{-4}/8.0 \approx 6.8 \times 10^{-5}\text{ s cm}^{-1}$.

hints: Wavelength is unchanged, so what stays the same on the trace - the horizontal spacing or the height? Think about what frequency controls.
Intensity $I$ is proportional to (amplitude)$^2$. If $I$ halves, does amplitude halve? Work out the factor $1/\sqrt{2} \approx 0.71$ for the new height.
walkthrough:
**Keep the timing the same**
Wavelength and speed are unchanged, so $f$ is unchanged. Your sketch must have peaks and troughs at the same horizontal positions as Fig. 4.1.

**Reduce the amplitude correctly**
For a wave, $$I \propto A^{2}$$ Halving $I$ gives: $$A_{new} = \frac{A_{old}}{\sqrt{2}} \approx 0.71 A_{old}$$ So draw the same sine shape but about 70 percent as tall, centred on the same line. A common mistake is to halve the height - that would quarter the intensity.
Final answer: Same period / same horizontal positions, with reduced peak height about 0.71 of original. Intensity $\propto A^{2}$ so $A_{new}=A/\sqrt{2}$.

hints: Loud sound means resonance - a stationary wave fits in the air column. Think how much longer the air column must get to fit the next resonance.
walkthrough:
**Successive resonances**
Level A is the first resonance where the air length is $\lambda/4$. The next loud point is when the length is $3\lambda/4$. The increase is: $$\Delta L = 3\lambda/4 - \lambda/4 = \lambda/2$$ So $$\Delta L = 0.18/2 = 0.090\text{ m}$$

hints: Remember where air cannot move - at the liquid surface (closed end) there must be a node, and at the open top there is an antinode.
walkthrough:
**Where nodes sit**
You have an open-closed tube. The liquid is a hard boundary so displacement is zero there - a node N. The top is open - an antinode. When the length is $3\lambda/4$ there are two nodes: one at the surface at level B, and one half a wavelength above it, i.e. $0.090\text{ m}$ higher up the tube.
Final answer: Label N at the liquid surface (level B) and a second N $\lambda/2$ ($0.09\text{ m}$) above it in the air column.

hints: First find the volume of liquid lost between A and B from the tube area and your distance from (c)(i). Remember to keep cm and m consistent.
Convert that volume to mass using density $\rho = m/V$, then use the mass loss rate to get time $t = m / (m/t)$.
walkthrough:
**Volume then mass between A and B**
Distance $h = 0.090\text{ m} = 9.0\text{ cm}$. $$V = A h = 13 \times 9.0 = 117\text{ cm}^{3}$$ $$m = \rho V = 0.79 \times 117 \approx 92\text{ g}$$

**Time from flow rate**
Mass leaves at $6.7\text{ g s}^{-1}$: $$t = \frac{m}{\text{rate}} = \frac{92.4}{6.7} \approx 13.8\text{ s} \approx 14\text{ s}$$
